title: Keep the shipment journal's lines whole

blocks.text: The depot's scanner workers record every parcel event in `ShipmentJournal`, many threads at once, and a flusher copies the journal to disk. The journal is a `StringBuffer`, picked because it is thread-safe, yet the night shift's file has lines such as `parcel=NL-5531 depot=parcel=BE-0907 depot=ANR-2 grams=610`. Looking up an event's depot can take a moment, because it asks another service.

Write `record(...)` in `src/main/java/practice/ShipmentJournal.java`. When you're done, every line in the journal is exactly one event's line, however the threads overlap, and a thread waiting on a slow depot lookup doesn't stop the other threads from recording. About four lines.
The tests make one event's lookup wait while another thread records, so the overlap happens on every run.

cases.says: each recorded event becomes one line of the journal, in the order recorded
while one thread is part-way through an event, a line recorded by another thread still reaches the journal whole
a thread waiting on a slow lookup does not block the other threads' records
the slow event's own line comes out whole too, with no text from the other event in it, and each event is written once

origin.section: StringBuffer Locks Each Call, So a Line Built from Several Calls Still Interleaves

concepts: StringBuffer makes each method call atomic, so a line written with several calls to a shared buffer can be interleaved with another thread's; building the line locally and appending it in one call keeps it whole.
Where several calls on a shared object must stay together, the text is built before the lock is taken, so a slow part of one record doesn't hold up the other threads.
One StringBuilder shared between threads, even a scratch builder cleared before each use, mixes or loses their text, and can throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
